chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from Salih ibn Abi Hammad, from one of his companions, from Yunus, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and Al-Husayn ibn Khalid, from Abu Al-Hasan Al-Reza (peace be upon him), and Sabbah al-Hazza', from Is'haq ibn Ammar, from Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him), regarding the man who goes to the animal.

They all said: If the animal belonged to the doer, it would be slaughtered; so when it is dead, it would be burnt with fire and no benefit would be taken from it, and he would be struck with twenty-five lashes, which is a quarter of the penalty (hadd) of the adulterer. And if the animal did not belong to him, it would be evaluated, its price taken from him, and given to its owner; and it would be slaughtered, burnt with fire, no benefit taken from it, and he would be struck with twenty-five lashes.

So I said, 'And what is the sin of the animal?' He said: 'It has no sin, but the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) did this and ordered it, so that people would not be bold with the animals and the lineage would be cut off.'

key_terms.الْبَهِيمَةُ: The animal (specifically in the context of bestiality)
key_terms.يَنْقَطِعَ النَّسْلُ: The lineage would be cut off

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling and punishment for bestiality according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the hadd punishment of twenty-five lashes for bestiality, mirroring the penalty for unmarried fornication, while prescribing the slaughter and burning of the animal to preserve its value for the owner. The Imam explains that the animal itself bears no sin, but the Prophet’s command to burn it serves a pragmatic legal purpose: to deter boldness and prevent the extinction of livestock lineages. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on both retributive justice and public interest (maslaha) in maintaining social and economic order.
